title: Research what educators in Africa need from a learning chat tool by Sun Nov 8
description: Audience: bootcamp founders, lecturers and school admins in Nigeria and the rest of Africa. Sources: public posts, forums, surveys and reports, with links for every claim. Done = the top 10 needs or pain points with evidence (e.g. data costs, phone-only learners, unreliable power, WhatsApp overload), which Zedu features answer each one, and 3 gaps Zedu doesn't cover yet.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Answer the question from the tools people already pay for: what they replace and what they still miss
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A different way at the same answer: start from the products African educators already use to run cohorts (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Google Classroom, Moodle, school LMSs) and gather what users say those tools do well and fail at - public app-store reviews, public community threads, and the support questions each tool answers publicly. That gives the needs in the buyer's own words, with links, and it is the same language Zedu's comparison and search pages need. Then map each need to the Zedu feature that answers it (channels, Buzz, file management, threads - all live pages), name the 3 needs Zedu does not cover, and add what a switch would cost in effort, which is the objection that decides most purchases. Every claim carries a link and a date; nothing is inferred from marketing copy alone.

upvotes.reason: Specific deliverable with a clear scope, a named owner for the result and a way to verify it was done properly.
Public reviews and community questions can provide linked evidence in educators’ own words; mapping each need to a verified feature and naming uncovered needs makes the result actionable for Zedu.
Starts from the tools educators already pay for and what they say fails

Starts from tools African educators already use, such as WhatsApp and Moodle, and gathers public reviews and threads, which fits the goal's rule of public sources with links. It maps needs to live Zedu features and names the gaps.
Grounding research in the actual software budgets African educators allocate reveals the exact switching triggers for Zedu.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Ask educators directly, then check the answers against the public record
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Public posts show what people say; short conversations show what they actually struggle with. (1) Run 12-15 short interviews (20 minutes) or one tight survey with bootcamp founders, lecturers and school admins, recruited from public communities across Nigeria plus two or three other African countries, covering data cost, phone-only learning, unreliable power, WhatsApp group overload, and what they use today. Consent is asked for up front and it is said plainly that this is research for Zedu. (2) Put the answers beside the public evidence from forums and reports and produce one ranked table: need, how many sources raised it, one representative quote, link, and severity. (3) Map each need to the Zedu feature that answers it, with the live page link, then name 3 gaps Zedu does not cover. Deliverables: interview guide and consent line, the transcripts or survey results, the combined ranked top 10, and the 3 gaps.

upvotes.reason: Has a scriptable structure, so it can be produced and checked rather than left open-ended.
Adds primary interviews with a consent line on top of the public evidence, which the goal's 'needs' question benefits from. It works well alongside the desk research.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Evidence mine first: real educator complaints from public posts, forums and reports
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Start from what educators have already said in public, so the top 10 rests on quotes and links rather than opinion. (1) Search public sources for bootcamp founders, lecturers and school admins describing problems with chat or teaching tools: Reddit, X and LinkedIn posts, Nairaland, Quora, Hacker News, Facebook groups, app-store reviews of WhatsApp/Slack for teaching, and published reports on digital education in Africa. (2) Save every quote with its link and date, group them into needs (data cost, phone-only learners, unreliable power, WhatsApp overload and the rest), count how often each appears, and rank the top 10. (3) Map each need to the Zedu feature that answers it with the live page link (channels, Buzz, file management, threads), then name 3 gaps Zedu does not cover yet and say plainly what evidence would close them. Every claim carries a source; nothing from memory. Deliverables: the sourced top-10 table, the feature match, and the 3 gaps.

upvotes.reason: Produces evidence the team can act on instead of opinion, and every claim would carry its source, so the result holds up under checking.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Measure the constraints with published data, reuse the project's research, and map needs to features in the app's code
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Complaints show what hurts; published datasets show how widespread it is. Plan: 1) for the constraints the goal names (data cost, phone-only learners, unreliable power), take the figures from primary sources such as the ITU and A4AI mobile-data price data, GSMA mobile connectivity reports and World Bank electricity-access data, per country, with the year of each figure; 2) add the educator needs already evidenced in this project (the operator problem bank, the African university LMS audit, the cohort objections work), cited to those deliveries, so nothing is researched twice; 3) map each of the top 10 to the Zedu feature that answers it, checked in the production code (Cybertron-HNG/zedu-fe, cybertron-integration), not only the marketing pages, and name 3 gaps, for example features the pricing page lists that the app doesn't have yet. Tasks: constraint figures by country (research), consolidated top-10 with feature map and gaps (research).

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Separate shared educator needs from country-specific needs before prioritising
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Use the evidence already collected for this goal and tag each item by country, role (bootcamp founder, lecturer, school admin or learner), and source type. Show which needs recur across roles and countries, which are local constraints, and how many independent sources support each finding. Then rank the top 10 by frequency and severity without treating a single anecdote as a widespread need. Deliver a cross-country matrix, confidence note for each finding, and a short priority list showing which Zedu feature or product gap relates to it. This turns the research into decisions about what to say and build, and complements the existing source-gathering approaches.
